title: How Wine Fraud Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore wine fraud: the history of fake wine, the Tesco knock-off Louis Jadot story, and the debate over how widespread counterfeiting is. They profile billionaire collector Bill Koch, who says he bought hundreds of fake bottles, and counterfeiter Rudy Kurniawan, who was convicted and sentenced to ten years after faking vintage Burgundy at auction. They also cover Hardy Rodenstock and his allegedly fake Thomas Jefferson bottles, including the engraving punctuation clue and cesium-137 dating, and methods of prevention such as RFID tags, tamper-evident capsules, and DNA-marked labels. The episode ends with a Facebook question segment covering research sources, favorite beers, favorite cities, pop tarts, and more.

segments.title: Opening banter and wine fraud intro
segments.summary: The hosts open with casual banter about coffee smells, then turn to wine fraud, citing a Tesco store selling counterfeit Louis Jadot and noting that the extent of wine fraud is hard to pin down.

segments.title: History of fake wine and wine tasting skepticism
segments.summary: The hosts trace fake wine back to ancient Rome, where lead was added to sweeten wine, and mention an urban legend about a 1980s Ruinart-style sweetener scare. They discuss whether wine tasters can really tell wines apart and how collectors' prior experience with fakes can skew their judgment.

segments.title: Vintage wine collecting and status
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why many collectors buy old bottles mainly for status and display rather than drinking them, which makes counterfeits harder to detect.

segments.title: Bill Koch and his collection
segments.summary: The hosts introduce billionaire Bill Koch, who collects guns, art and wine and says he owns several hundred bottles he suspects are fake. A random sample of 3,000 bottles reportedly yielded 130 fakes, and he has sued many sellers.

segments.title: Rudy Kurniawan's counterfeiting
segments.summary: The hosts describe Rudy Kurniawan, who was sentenced to ten years and ordered to pay about fifty million dollars. They describe how he built a reputation with lavish restaurant parties and Acker Merrall connections, bought old vintages, and was caught after a Ponsot Clos Saint-Denis mistake. He is appealing his conviction.

segments.title: Whether wine fraud affects ordinary drinkers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether counterfeit vintage wine affects regular wine buyers, concluding the vintage and everyday wine markets are largely separate, though fraud still costs people money and reputations.

segments.title: Two ways to fake wine and Lafite examples
segments.summary: The hosts explain that fakers either refill a real bottle with other wine or put a real wine in a fake or altered bottle. They discuss Kurniawan's methods, the difficulty of obtaining old mediocre vintages, and the Lafite labels he altered. They also share personal wine preferences.

segments.title: Hardy Rodenstock and the Jefferson bottles
segments.summary: The hosts profile Hardy Rodenstock, allegedly a counterfeiter who sold Thomas Jefferson bottles to billionaires like Bill Koch and Christopher Forbes. The sales were allegedly tied to a punctuation mismatch in the engraved initials, a cesium-137 test, and a former tenant's account. Rodenstock has denied the allegations and the cases are civil, not criminal.

segments.title: Preventing wine fraud and the eBay problem
segments.summary: The hosts describe anti-counterfeiting methods such as RFID tags, QR codes, tamper-evident neck capsules, and DNA-marked label ink. They also discuss empty vintage bottles sold on eBay and Chateau Lafleur magnum counts that suggest fakes.

segments.title: Counterfeit market shifting to China
segments.summary: The hosts note that as American buyers grow more savvy, the counterfeit wine market is reportedly moving to China, where wealth is growing and wine education is limited.

segments.title: Wine fraud wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the wine fraud discussion and recommend searching How Stuff Works for more.

segments.title: Facebook questions and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts answer Facebook questions about research sources, favorite beers and homebrewing, favorite cities, pop tart flavors, and what they would measure as units, then sign off with contact information.
